EMPLOYEE POLITICAL ACTIVITY PROTECTION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE
Acme, Inc. provides this information sheet to Jordan Lee to describe the California statutory protections for employees' political activities and affiliations set out in Labor Code sections 1101 through 1106, including the core prohibition on employer rules or policies restricting political activity, the separate prohibition on coercing employees through threat of discharge, how California courts have construed the scope of "political activity" under these statutes, and the penalties and remedies the statute itself provides. This information sheet states general rules of California law. It is not a statement of Acme, Inc.'s policies or practices, and it does not describe whether any particular conduct by Jordan Lee or Acme, Inc. does or does not fall within these statutes.

THE CORE PROHIBITION ON EMPLOYER RULES RESTRICTING POLITICAL ACTIVITY
California Labor Code section 1101 prohibits an employer from making, adopting, or enforcing any rule, regulation, or policy that either (a) forbids or prevents employees from engaging or participating in politics or from becoming candidates for public office, or (b) controls or directs, or tends to control or direct, the political activities or affiliations of employees.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "No employer shall make, adopt, or enforce any rule, regulation, or policy: (a) Forbidding or preventing employees from engaging or participating in politics or from becoming candidates for public office. (b) Controlling or directing, or tending to control or direct the political activities or affiliations of employees."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1101 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, Chapter 5 (Political Affiliations), Part 3, Division 2 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1101.)
  Known gap: Section 1101 does not itself define "political activity" or "political activities or affiliations"; how California courts have construed those terms is addressed in a separate clause of this document. This clause states the statute's own text; it does not determine whether any particular rule, regulation, policy, or practice of the employer does or does not fall within section 1101's prohibition, which is a fact-specific question this document does not resolve.

A SEPARATE PROHIBITION ON COERCING EMPLOYEES' POLITICAL CHOICES
California Labor Code section 1102 separately prohibits an employer from coercing or influencing, or attempting to coerce or influence, employees, through or by means of threat of discharge or loss of employment, to adopt or follow, or refrain from adopting or following, any particular course or line of political action or political activity. This is a distinct prohibition from the one stated in section 1101: section 1101 addresses employer rules, regulations, or policies restricting political activity generally, while section 1102 addresses the specific mechanism of coercing or influencing employees through the threat of discharge or loss of employment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "No employer shall coerce or influence or attempt to coerce or influence his employees through or by means of threat of discharge or loss of employment to adopt or follow or refrain from adopting or following any particular course or line of political action or political activity."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1102 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, Chapter 5 (Political Affiliations), Part 3, Division 2 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1102.)
  Known gap: This clause cites section 1102 alone; the comparison it draws to section 1101 is addressed with its own citation in a separate clause of this document, so the two are not combined here as though verified by a single source. This clause states the statute's own text; it does not determine whether any particular statement or action by the employer does or does not amount to coercion or influence within the meaning of section 1102, which is a fact-specific question this document does not resolve.

HOW THE CALIFORNIA SUPREME COURT HAS CONSTRUED "POLITICAL ACTIVITY" UNDER THESE STATUTES
Neither section 1101 nor section 1102 defines "political activity." The California Supreme Court has held that sections 1101 and 1102 serve to protect "the fundamental right of employees in general to engage in political activity without interference by employers," and that these statutes "cannot be narrowly confined to partisan activity" such as voting or campaign work. The Supreme Court approved a description of "political activity" as connoting "the espousal of a candidate or a cause, and some degree of action to promote the acceptance thereof by other persons." Applying that description, the Supreme Court held that a complaint alleging an employer discriminated against employees who identified themselves as members of an advocacy movement and worked to advance its cause stated a claim under sections 1101 and 1102.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "These sections serve to protect “the fundamental right of employees in general to engage in political activity without interference by employers.”"
  — Gay Law Students Assn. v. Pacific Tel. & Tel. Co., 24 Cal.3d 458, 487 (1979) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1365592/gay-law-students-assn-v-pacific-telephone-telegraph-co/)
  "These statutes cannot be narrowly confined to partisan activity."
  — Gay Law Students Assn. v. Pacific Tel. & Tel. Co., 24 Cal.3d 458, 487 (1979) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1365592/gay-law-students-assn-v-pacific-telephone-telegraph-co/)
  "The term ‘political activity’ connotes the espousal of a candidate or a cause, and some degree of action to promote the acceptance thereof by other persons."
  — Gay Law Students Assn. v. Pacific Tel. & Tel. Co., quoting Mallard v. Boring (1960) 182 Cal.App.2d 390, 395, 24 Cal.3d 458, 487 (1979) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1365592/gay-law-students-assn-v-pacific-telephone-telegraph-co/)
  Known gap: Both quotations in this clause are drawn from the same single opinion, Gay Law Students Assn. v. Pacific Tel. & Tel. Co. (1979) 24 Cal.3d 458 -- the "fundamental right" and "not narrowly confined to partisan activity" language, and the "espousal of a candidate or a cause" description (which that opinion in turn quotes from an earlier Court of Appeal decision, Mallard v. Boring (1960) 182 Cal.App.2d 390) -- so they are not independent of one another; only one source was independently fetched and verified for this clause. This is a single, on-point California Supreme Court construction of these statutes, not an exhaustive catalogue of every activity that has been or could be held to qualify as "political activity," and it does not determine whether any specific activity by the employee does or does not qualify for this statutory protection in a particular case.

THE PENALTIES AND CIVIL REMEDY THIS CHAPTER ITSELF PROVIDES
This chapter of the Labor Code states its own penalty and remedy. On the criminal side, an employer, or any other person or entity, that violates the chapter is guilty of a misdemeanor, punishable -- in the case of an individual -- by imprisonment in the county jail not to exceed one year, a fine not to exceed one thousand dollars, or both, and -- in the case of a corporation -- by a fine not to exceed five thousand dollars. On the civil side, the chapter states that nothing in it prevents an injured employee from recovering damages from the employer for injury suffered through a violation of the chapter. Consistent with that text, the California Supreme Court has recognized that an employee discriminated against in violation of sections 1101 or 1102 may maintain a civil cause of action against the employer to recover damages sustained from the employer's unlawful conduct.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "An employer or any other person or entity that violates this chapter is guilty of a misdemeanor punishable, in the case of an individual, by imprisonment in the county jail not to exceed one year or a fine not to exceed one thousand dollars ($1,000) or both that fine and imprisonment, or, in the case of a corporation, by a fine not to exceed five thousand dollars ($5,000)."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1103 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, Chapter 5 (Political Affiliations), Part 3, Division 2 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1103.)
  "Nothing in this chapter shall prevent the injured employee from recovering damages from his employer for injury suffered through a violation of this chapter."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1105 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, Chapter 5 (Political Affiliations), Part 3, Division 2 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1105.)
  "our court established the principle that an employee who has been discriminated against in violation of sections 1101 or 1102 may maintain a cause of action against his employer to recover damages sustained as a result of the employer’s unlawful conduct."
  — Gay Law Students Assn. v. Pacific Tel. & Tel. Co., 24 Cal.3d 458, 488-89 (1979) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1365592/gay-law-students-assn-v-pacific-telephone-telegraph-co/)
  Known gap: This clause draws on two genuinely separate, independently-numbered sections of the same chapter -- section 1103 (the criminal misdemeanor penalty) and section 1105 (the statement preserving an injured employee's ability to recover civil damages) -- together with California Supreme Court case law (Gay Law Students Assn. v. Pacific Tel. & Tel. Co. (1979) 24 Cal.3d 458, 488-89) recognizing a civil damages action consistent with section 1105's text; that Supreme Court discussion in turn cites, but this clause does not independently verify, an earlier decision, Lockheed Aircraft Corp. v. Superior Court (1946) 28 Cal.2d 481. This document does not state that any misdemeanor charge would in fact be brought, or that any particular employer conduct would in fact expose it to criminal or civil liability under this chapter -- those are fact-specific and prosecutorial-discretion questions this document does not resolve. Section 1104 (employer responsibility, in a prosecution under this chapter, for the acts of its managers, officers, agents, and employees) and section 1106 (which extends the chapter's "employee" definition to certain public-sector workers, but only for purposes of sections 1102.5, 1102.6, 1102.7, 1102.8, 1104, and 1105 -- not for purposes of sections 1101, 1102, or 1103 themselves) were also verified but are not restated in the body of this clause.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
By signing below, the undersigned acknowledge that this information sheet was provided and that it states general rules of California law about employees' political activities under Labor Code sections 1101 through 1106 and their judicial construction, rather than advice about Jordan Lee's specific circumstances or Acme, Inc.'s specific policies, practices, or legal obligations.

Title: _______________
Date: September 1, 2026
